# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

MANUFACTURERS' SHIPMENTS, INVENTORIES, & ORDERS

About the Surveys

PURPOSE

The purpose of the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) survey is to provide broad-based monthly statistical data on current economic conditions and indications of future production commitments in the manufacturing sector.

COVERAGE

The M3 is based upon data reported from manufacturing establishments with $500 million or more in annual shipments. Units may be divisions of diversified large companies, large homogenous companies, or single-unit manufacturers in 89 industry categories.

CONTENT

The M3 provides statistics on manufacturers' value of shipments, new orders (net of cancellations), end-of-month order backlog (unfilled orders), end-of-month total inventory, materials and supplies, work-in-process, and finished goods inventories (at current cost or market value). Data are collected and tabulated predominantly by 6-digit NAICS (North American Industry Classification System).

FREQUENCY

The survey has been conducted monthly by the US Census Bureau since 1957.

METHODS

Data are collected by FAX image capture (PFIRS) and Internet-based survey form (Census Taker). Data describe activities taking place during the calendar month.

PRODUCTS

There are two press releases per month. The first, Advance Report on Durable Goods Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders is available about 18 working days after each month. The second, Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders includes durable and non-durable manufacturing and is available about 23 working days after each month.

USES

Bureau of Economic Analysis uses M3 data to make GDP estimates and compiles the principal economic indicator series. The Federal Reserve Board, Department of Treasury, Council of Economic Advisers develop fiscal and monetary policy. Corporate economists, trade associations, news media, academia, investment consultants, and researchers use M3 data for analysis and forecasting of future economic conditions.

CONFIDENTIALITY

The U.S. Census Bureau is required by Section 9 of Title 13 United States Code to keep respondents' information confidential and can use the information only to produce statistics. The Census Bureau is not permitted to publicly release a respondent's information in a way that could identify a business, organization, or institution. Per the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015, submitted data are protected from cybersecurity risks through screening of the systems that transmit the data.

[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 137 (Monday, July 20, 2026)]

[Pages 45236-45237]
From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]
[FR Doc No: 2026-14513]



[[Page 45236]]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and Orders (M3) 
Survey

AGENCY: Census Bureau, Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of information collection, request for comment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork 
Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information 
collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information 
collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. The 
purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment on the 
proposed extension of the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and 
Orders (M3) survey, prior to the submission of the information 
collection request (ICR) to OMB for approval.

DATES: To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed 
information collection must be received on or before September 18, 
2026.

ADDRESSES: Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by 
email to [email protected]. Please reference the Manufacturers' 
Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) Survey in the subject line of 
your comments. You may also submit comments, identified by Docket 
Number USBC-2026-0265, to the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov. All comments received are part of the public 
record. No comments will be posted to http://www.regulations.gov for 
public viewing until after the comment period has closed. Comments will 
generally be posted without change. All Personally Identifiable 
Information (for example, name and address) voluntarily submitted by 
the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do not submit Confidential 
Business Information or otherwise sensitive or protected information. 
You may submit attachments to electronic comments in Microsoft Word, 
Excel, or Adobe PDF file formats.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Requests for additional information or 
specific questions related to collection activities should be directed 
to Carol Aristone, Assistant Division Chief, Economic Indicators 
Division, (301) 763-7062, [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Abstract

    The U.S. Census Bureau plans to request an extension of the current 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) clearance of the Manufacturers' 
Shipments, Inventories and Orders (M3) survey. The M3 survey requests 
data monthly from domestic manufacturers on form M-3 (SD). Data 
requested are shipments, new orders, unfilled orders, total inventory, 
materials and supplies, work-in-process, and finished goods.
    The M3 survey is designed to measure current industrial activity 
and to provide an indication of future production commitments. The 
value of shipments measures the value of goods delivered during the 
month by domestic manufacturers. Estimates of new orders serve as an 
indicator of future production commitments and represent the current 
sales value of new orders received during the month, net of 
cancellations. Substantial accumulation or depletion of unfilled orders 
measures excess or deficient demand for manufactured products. The 
level of inventories, especially in relation to shipments, is 
frequently used to monitor the business cycle, by calculating the 
inventories to sales ratio. In general, a low ratio indicates strong 
shipments. A high ratio indicates weaker shipments or accumulation of 
inventories in stock.
    In October 2021, we accelerated total manufacturing and the 
nondurable manufacturing aggregate estimates to the same time as the 
Advance Report on Durable Goods Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories 
and Orders by creating an advance high-level report of total 
manufacturing. This exception to the normal procedure was initially 
approved by Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in September 2021 and 
was extended annually through means of a separately submitted memo. In 
2024, the Census Bureau requested and OMB approved the provisions for 
the early release of total manufacturing shipments, inventories and 
orders to be included in the clearance, thereby eliminating the need 
for a separate annual re-approval from OMB for the early release. This 
early data has permitted the public release of preliminary monthly data 
on shipments and inventories of total manufacturing under the 
provisions of the OMB's Statistical Policy Directive No. 3 on the 
Compilation, Release, and Evaluation of Principal Federal Economic 
Indicators. Currently, the Advance Report on Durable Goods is available 
approximately 18 working days after each month, with the full report 
available approximately 23 working days after each month. Accelerating 
the nondurable release provides data users with early access to total 
manufacturing estimates ahead of the full report, giving them an early 
snapshot of the direction of this critical indicator. In 2024, we 
included additional nondurable goods industry level data. In July 2024, 
advance data included petroleum and coal products shipments and 
inventories, and in October 2024, estimates included the addition of 
the food products and chemical products early shipments and inventories 
from the monthly Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and Orders (M3) 
Survey. Additionally, in July 2025, the Advance Total Manufacturing 
publication included detailed shipments and inventories data for all 
nondurable industries, to provide more detail estimates at the advance 
time.

II. Method of Collection

    We collect the data primarily by internet. Respondents are 
initially contacted by email, with a small subset receiving a letter by 
mail. Paper collection has been phased out since January 2026. 
Respondents may submit their data via the internet or email. We send 
emails and make telephone calls to respondents to remind them to report 
on time.

III. Data

    OMB Control Number: 0607-0008.
    Form Number(s): M-3 (SD).
    Type of Review: Regular submission, Request for an Extension, 
without Change, of a Currently Approved Collection.
    Affected Public: Manufacturing Business or other for-profit 
organizations.
    Estimated Number of Respondents: 5,000 respondents filing a total 
of 60,000 reports per year.
    Estimated Time per Response: 20 minutes.
    Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours: 20,000.
    Estimated Total Annual Cost to Public: $0. (This is not the cost of 
respondents' time, but the indirect costs respondents may incur for 
such things as purchases of specialized software or hardware needed to 
report, or expenditures for accounting or records maintenance services 
required specifically by the collection.)
    Respondent's Obligation: Voluntary.
    Legal Authority: Title 13 U.S.C. 131, 182, and 193.

[[Page 45237]]

IV. Request for Comments

    We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department/Bureau 
to: (a) Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is 
necessary for the proper functions of the Department, including whether 
the information will have practical utility; (b) Evaluate the accuracy 
of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed 
collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions 
used; (c) Evaluate ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of 
the information to be collected; and (d) Minimize the reporting burden 
on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection 
techniques or other forms of information technology.
    Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of 
public record. We will include, or summarize, each comment in our 
request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, 
phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information 
in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment--
including your personal identifying information--may be made publicly 
available at any time. While you may ask us in your comment to withhold 
your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot 
guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Sheleen Dumas,
Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

The Secretary shall take, compile, and publish censuses of manufactures, of mineral industries, and of other businesses, including the distributive trades, service establishments, and transportation (exclusive of means of transportation for which statistics are required by law to be filed with, and are compiled and published by, a designated regulatory body), in the year 1964, then in the year 1968, and every fifth year thereafter, and each such census shall relate to the year immediately preceding the taking thereof.

(Aug. 31, 1954, ch. 1158, 68 Stat. 1019; Pub. L. 85–207, § 8, Aug. 28, 1957, 71 Stat. 482; Pub. L. 88–532, Aug. 31, 1964, 78 Stat. 737.)
Historical and Revision Notes

Based on title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., § 121 (June 19, 1948, ch. 502, § 1, 62 Stat. 478; June 18, 1954, ch. 315, 68 Stat. 258).

Section was subsection (a) of section 121 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed. The remainder of such section 121, which constituted subsection (b) thereof, is incorporated in subchapter IV of this chapter.

At the beginning, “The Secretary”, meaning the Secretary of Commerce, was substituted for a reference to the Director of the Bureau of the Census, and, at the end, the provision that the territorial scope of the censuses should be determined by the Secretary was substituted for the provision of section 121 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., that such determination should be made by the Director with the approval of the Secretary, to conform with 1950 Reorganization Plan No. 5, §§ 1, 2, eff. May 24, 1950, 15 F.R. 3174, 64 Stat. 1263, which transferred all functions of all officers and employees, agencies and bureaus of the Department of Commerce to the Secretary. However, the Secretary, under that plan, may delegate any of such transferred functions, as well as any other of his functions, to any of such officers, employees, agencies and bureaus. See, also, section 4 of this title.

The reference in section 121 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., to the year “1949” as the year for commencement of the quinquennial censuses was changed to the year “1954”, since the former designation is obsolete, and the provision of such section that the census of manufacturers should not be taken in 1949 was omitted as obsolete.

Changes were made in phraseology.

Editorial Notes
Amendments

1964—Pub. L. 88–532 substituted “in the year 1964, then in the year 1968, and” for “in the year 1954 and” and struck out provisions which related to the taking of certain censuses in the year 1955.

1957—Pub. L. 85–207 struck out sentence which included the United States and its territories and such possessions as the Secretary might determine in the censuses to be taken. See section 191 of this title.

Statutory Notes and Related Subsidiaries
Census Data on Women Owned Businesses; Study and Report

Pub. L. 100–533, title V, § 501, Oct. 25, 1988, 102 Stat. 2697, provided that:

“(a) Bureau of Labor Statistics.—The Bureau of Labor Statistics of the Department of Labor shall include in any census report it may prepare on women owned business data on—
“(1)
sole proprietorships;
“(2)
partnerships; and
“(3)
corporations.
“(b) Bureau of the Census.—
The Bureau of the Census of the Department of Commerce shall include in its Business Census for 1992 and each such succeeding census data on the number of corporations which are 51 per centum or more owned by women.
“(c) Combined Study.—
Not later than one hundred and eighty days after the effective date of this section [Oct. 25, 1988], the Office of the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration (hereinafter referred to in this subsection as the ‘Office’) shall conduct a study and prepare a report recommending the most cost effective and accurate means to gather and present the data required to be collected pursuant to subsections (a) and (b). The Department of Commerce and the Department of Labor shall provide the Office such assistance and cooperation as may be necessary and appropriate to achieve the purposes of this subsection.”

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau

September 2, 2025 – March 19, 2026 IF13105

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau
Updated March 19, 2026 (IF13105)

Introduction

As a Department of Commerce agency, the U.S. Census Bureau is primarily funded through the annual Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS) appropriations bill. This In Focus provides an overview of FY2026 appropriations for the U.S. Census Bureau; certain comparisons to previous years' appropriations; and congressional action to date. Information presented is drawn from the Census Bureau's FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification, the enacted FY2026 CJS bill, and other relevant congressional documents.

The FY2026 appropriations are divided between two accounts: Current Surveys and Programs, and Periodic Censuses and Programs. For these two accounts, comparisons are made here between the FY2026 enacted level, the FY2026 request, and enacted amounts for FY2024 and FY2025. (The FY2025 full-year continuing resolution [CR] funded these accounts in the same amounts and under the same authorities and conditions as enacted in FY2024.) The FY2026 budget justification also includes requested amounts below the account level in more detail, which are compared here to corresponding actual FY2024 amounts (the budget justification document does not provide this level of detail for FY2025 actual amounts).

Figure 1. Census Budget Authority

Source: Data from U.S. Census Bureau, FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification and FY2026 Appropriations.

Notes: Values may not add evenly due to rounding.

FY2026 Appropriations

The enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) includes $1.490 billion for the Census Bureau. This is $186 million less than the Trump Administration's FY2026 budget request of $1.677 billion and a $108 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted levels of $1.383 billion.

Current Surveys and Programs

The bill includes $319 million for the Current Surveys and Programs account, which is $30 million above the Administration's FY2026 requested $289 million and a decrease of $10 million from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amounts of $329 million. This account includes funding for Current Economic Statistics and Current Demographic Statistics.

Current Economic Statistics

Current Economic Statistics include business, construction, manufacturing, general economic, foreign trade, and government statistics. According to the FY2026 budget justification, Current Economic Statistics programs "provide timely, accurate, and essential data on the structure and performance of the U.S. economy, supporting the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimation, fiscal and monetary policymaking, and private sector decision-making."

The FY2026 request for Current Economic Statistics was $216 million, the same as FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts.

Current Demographic Statistics

Current Demographic Statistics includes the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP); the Current Population Survey (CPS), which is sponsored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the Census Bureau; and the Population Estimates Program. The SIPP is an ongoing survey that measures distribution of government assistance programs. The CPS provides estimates of income, poverty, and other indicators. The Population Estimates Program calculates population change over time. The Census Bureau's population estimates are used in a variety of federal programs to determine funding allocations or eligibility.

The FY2026 request for Current Demographic Statistics was $73 million, which is a $40 million decrease from FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts of $113 million.

Proposed changes to these programs include testing internet self-response for the CPS and using some nonsurvey data to reduce costs for the SIPP.

Periodic Censuses and Programs

The bill includes $1.172 billion for the Periodic Censuses and Programs account, which is $216 million less than the Administration's FY2026 requested $1.388 billion and a $118 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amount of $1.054 billion. This account consists of funding for several programs discussed below.

Decennial Census

The FY2026 request for the decennial census account was $983 million, a $383 million increase from the FY2024 actual amount of $600 million. Requested FY2026 funding for the decennial census includes support for the 2026 Census Test and preparation for the 2028 Dress Rehearsal, full-scale development of core IT infrastructure, award and management of contracts, and continued data collection and publication for the American Community Survey (ACS). Unlike previous budget documents, the FY2026 budget justification does not specify the respective amounts for the 2030 decennial census and the ACS within the decennial census account.

Periodic Economic Statistics

The FY2026 request for the Periodic Economic Statistics Program, which contains the Economic Census and the Census of Governments, was $144 million, an $18 million decrease from the FY2024 actual level of $162 million. Specific funding levels for these two surveys are not provided in the FY2026 budget request.

The Economic Census, conducted every five years, collects statistics on businesses in the United States to help understand the U.S. economy. Requested FY2026 activities for the Economic Census include the continued review of 2022 Economic Census data releases.

The Census of Governments, conducted every five years, collects statistics on state and local governments across the United States. Requested FY2026 activities for the Census of Governments include the expanded use of administrative records and other data collection methods in preparation for the 2027 Census of Governments.

Geographic Support Program

The purpose of the Census Bureau's Geographic Support Program (GSP) is to support and maintain the geospatial infrastructure required to conduct survey data collection, processing, tabulation, and dissemination across covered regions. The Census Bureau considers the GSP to be foundational for all of its social and economic data products. Congressional district wall maps are produced by the GSP. The Census Bureau aims to utilize the GSP to minimize 2030 Census in-field enumeration costs.

The FY2026 request for the GSP was $98 million, a $14 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $112 million.

Enterprise Data Collection and Dissemination Systems (EDCaDS)

The EDCaDS generally supports the data collection, processing, and dissemination systems that are associated with Census Bureau programs.

The FY2026 request's stated goal for the EDCaDS is "to provide large cyclical systems that must be scaled for peak operations for the Decennial Census, the Economic Census, and the Census of Governments."

The FY2026 request for the EDCaDS was $163 million, a $17 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $180 million.

Congressional Action

The House Appropriations Committee CJS subcommittee marked up the House version of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 15, 2025. The bill, as approved by the subcommittee, would have provided $1.677 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $288.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.388 billion for Periodic Censuses and Programs. The bill, as reported, would have prohibited the Census Bureau from using any funds provided in the measure to include "aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States" in rendering apportionment determinations. It also included similar prohibitions on using any funds provided to enforce mandatory response requirements for certain Census Bureau surveys or to inquire more than twice to solicit voluntary survey responses. These provisions were not included in the version of the bill subsequently enacted into law. The bill advanced from the subcommittee by a 9-6 vote. The full committee ordered the bill reported by a 34-28 vote on September 10, 2025.

The Senate Appropriations Committee marked up its FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 17, 2025. The bill, as reported, would have provided $1.520 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $328.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.192 billion for Periodic Census and Programs. Furthermore, the committee report accompanying the bill directs the Census Bureau to provide information regarding the removal of Census and BEA data sets; the termination of Census Bureau advisory committees; ACS modernization efforts; 2030 decennial census operation plans; and the effects of field office closures. The report directs the Census Bureau to continue outreach to public libraries as partners for surveys and to prioritize carrying out the 2026 Census Test. The committee ordered the bill reported by a 19-10 vote.

Census Bureau appropriations lapsed from October 1 through November 12, 2025. The lapse ended when a CR providing appropriations for certain agencies (including the Commerce Department) through January 30, 2026, became law. The FY2026 CJS appropriations bill was included as part of a consolidated appropriations measure, which passed the House by a vote of 397-28 on January 8, 2026, and passed the Senate by a vote of 82-15 on January 15, 2026. The bill was signed into law by President Trump on January 23, 2026. The explanatory statement for the FY2026 CJS bill was filed in the Congressional Record by the chair of the House Appropriations Committee on January 8, 2026. The explanatory statement specifies that the Appropriations Committee reports accompanying the House and Senate versions of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill carry "the same weight as language included in this joint explanatory statement and should be complied with unless specifically addressed to the contrary in this joint explanatory statement or in the act."

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and Orders (M3) 
Survey

AGENCY: Census Bureau, Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of information collection, request for comment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork 
Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information 
collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information 
collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. The 
purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment on the 
proposed extension of the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and 
Orders (M3) survey, prior to the submission of the information 
collection request (ICR) to OMB for approval.

DATES: To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed 
information collection must be received on or before September 18, 
2026.

ADDRESSES: Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by 
email to [email protected]. Please reference the Manufacturers' 
Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) Survey in the subject line of 
your comments. You may also submit comments, identified by Docket 
Number USBC-2026-0265, to the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov. All comments received are part of the public 
record. No comments will be posted to http://www.regulations.gov for 
public viewing until after the comment period has closed. Comments will 
generally be posted without change. All Personally Identifiable 
Information (for example, name and address) voluntarily submitted by 
the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do not submit Confidential 
Business Information or otherwise sensitive or protected information. 
You may submit attachments to electronic comments in Microsoft Word, 
Excel, or Adobe PDF file formats.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Requests for additional information or 
specific questions related to collection activities should be directed 
to Carol Aristone, Assistant Division Chief, Economic Indicators 
Division, (301) 763-7062, [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Abstract

    The U.S. Census Bureau plans to request an extension of the current 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) clearance of the Manufacturers' 
Shipments, Inventories and Orders (M3) survey. The M3 survey requests 
data monthly from domestic manufacturers on form M-3 (SD). Data 
requested are shipments, new orders, unfilled orders, total inventory, 
materials and supplies, work-in-process, and finished goods.
    The M3 survey is designed to measure current industrial activity 
and to provide an indication of future production commitments. The 
value of shipments measures the value of goods delivered during the 
month by domestic manufacturers. Estimates of new orders serve as an 
indicator of future production commitments and represent the current 
sales value of new orders received during the month, net of 
cancellations. Substantial accumulation or depletion of unfilled orders 
measures excess or deficient demand for manufactured products. The 
level of inventories, especially in relation to shipments, is 
frequently used to monitor the business cycle, by calculating the 
inventories to sales ratio. In general, a low ratio indicates strong 
shipments. A high ratio indicates weaker shipments or accumulation of 
inventories in stock.
    In October 2021, we accelerated total manufacturing and the 
nondurable manufacturing aggregate estimates to the same time as the 
Advance Report on Durable Goods Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories 
and Orders by creating an advance high-level report of total 
manufacturing. This exception to the normal procedure was initially 
approved by Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in September 2021 and 
was extended annually through means of a separately submitted memo. In 
2024, the Census Bureau requested and OMB approved the provisions for 
the early release of total manufacturing shipments, inventories and 
orders to be included in the clearance, thereby eliminating the need 
for a separate annual re-approval from OMB for the early release. This 
early data has permitted the public release of preliminary monthly data 
on shipments and inventories of total manufacturing under the 
provisions of the OMB's Statistical Policy Directive No. 3 on the 
Compilation, Release, and Evaluation of Principal Federal Economic 
Indicators. Currently, the Advance Report on Durable Goods is available 
approximately 18 working days after each month, with the full report 
available approximately 23 working days after each month. Accelerating 
the nondurable release provides data users with early access to total 
manufacturing estimates ahead of the full report, giving them an early 
snapshot of the direction of this critical indicator. In 2024, we 
included additional nondurable goods industry level data. In July 2024, 
advance data included petroleum and coal products shipments and 
inventories, and in October 2024, estimates included the addition of 
the food products and chemical products early shipments and inventories 
from the monthly Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and Orders (M3) 
Survey. Additionally, in July 2025, the Advance Total Manufacturing 
publication included detailed shipments and inventories data for all 
nondurable industries, to provide more detail estimates at the advance 
time.

II. Method of Collection

    We collect the data primarily by internet. Respondents are 
initially contacted by email, with a small subset receiving a letter by 
mail. Paper collection has been phased out since January 2026. 
Respondents may submit their data via the internet or email. We send 
emails and make telephone calls to respondents to remind them to report 
on time.

III. Data

    OMB Control Number: 0607-0008.
    Form Number(s): M-3 (SD).
    Type of Review: Regular submission, Request for an Extension, 
without Change, of a Currently Approved Collection.
    Affected Public: Manufacturing Business or other for-profit 
organizations.
    Estimated Number of Respondents: 5,000 respondents filing a total 
of 60,000 reports per year.
    Estimated Time per Response: 20 minutes.
    Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours: 20,000.
    Estimated Total Annual Cost to Public: $0. (This is not the cost of 
respondents' time, but the indirect costs respondents may incur for 
such things as purchases of specialized software or hardware needed to 
report, or expenditures for accounting or records maintenance services 
required specifically by the collection.)
    Respondent's Obligation: Voluntary.
    Legal Authority: Title 13 U.S.C. 131, 182, and 193.

[[Page 45237]]

IV. Request for Comments

    We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department/Bureau 
to: (a) Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is 
necessary for the proper functions of the Department, including whether 
the information will have practical utility; (b) Evaluate the accuracy 
of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed 
collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions 
used; (c) Evaluate ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of 
the information to be collected; and (d) Minimize the reporting burden 
on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection 
techniques or other forms of information technology.
    Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of 
public record. We will include, or summarize, each comment in our 
request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, 
phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information 
in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment--
including your personal identifying information--may be made publicly 
available at any time. While you may ask us in your comment to withhold 
your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot 
guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Sheleen Dumas,
Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3)
Description: The Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) survey provides broad-based, monthly statistical data on economic conditions in the domestic manufacturing sector. The survey measures current industrial activity and provides an indication of future business trends.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Manufacturers’ Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3)

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Primary publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce  
**Overall assessment:** A long-running, nationally important monthly economic-statistics program. Its public products are aggregate estimates—not a census of every manufacturer or an openly downloadable business-level dataset.

## Executive findings

**Your title and description are accurate.** The description you supplied matches the Census Bureau’s description of the M3 survey. More precisely, M3 is a survey program that produces a family of datasets, time series, advance estimates, full reports, and benchmark revisions. [1]

The most important findings for researchers and preservationists are:

- **Purpose:** Measure current domestic manufacturing activity and provide indicators of future production commitments through shipments, inventories, new orders, and order backlogs.
- **Publisher:** Census Bureau’s **Economic Indicators Division, Shipments, Inventories, and Orders Branch**.
- **Authority:** **13 U.S.C. §§ 131, 182, and 193**. Participation in the monthly M3 survey is **voluntary**, despite its statutory authorization.
- **Statistical importance:** M3 is a **principal federal economic indicator**. It contributes to GDP estimation, business-cycle analysis, and fiscal and monetary policymaking.
- **History:** Census reports conducting the monthly survey since **1957**. Historical series have different starting dates and classification systems.
- **Major limitation:** The contemporary panel is **not a probability sample**. Census cannot calculate conventional sampling errors or confidence intervals for its published estimates.
- **Preservation priority:** Preserve **release vintages**, not just the latest historical series. Revisions change what users would have known at earlier dates.
- **Current operational concern:** Census states that, because of schedule and resource constraints, revised historical data and seasonal-adjustment models will remain unchanged for the remainder of **2026**. This is **not** a statement that monthly publication has stopped. [1, 4]
- **Documentation caution:** Some Census overview pages are outdated. Recent releases and Federal Register notices supersede their older descriptions of collection methods, industry counts, and advance products.

---

## 1. Dataset identity and scope

| Attribute | Findings |
|---|---|
| Official title | Manufacturers’ Shipments, Inventories, and Orders |
| Acronym | M3 |
| Resource type | Monthly business survey and associated aggregate statistical products |
| Subject | Domestic manufacturing economic activity |
| Geographic presentation | Primarily United States national totals and national industry estimates; not a standard state/county manufacturing dataset |
| Frequency | Monthly |
| Reference period | Calendar month; inventories and unfilled orders are end-of-period stocks |
| Public observational unit | An industry or aggregate series for a month, measure, and seasonal-adjustment status |
| Confidential reporting unit | Company or company division/reporting unit, sometimes encompassing multiple establishments |
| Main monetary units | Millions of current dollars in public tables; ratios and percentage changes have different units |
| Industry classification | NAICS-based M3 industry categories; historical SIC series also exist |
| Adjustment | Seasonally adjusted and not seasonally adjusted products |
| Inflation adjustment | **Not adjusted for price changes** |
| Collection identifier | OMB control number **0607-0008** |
| Questionnaire | **M-3(SD)** |

The program concerns **manufacturing operations located in the United States**, not simply companies with U.S. ownership. The questionnaire includes shipments to foreign customers as well as domestic customers and transfers to other company divisions.

Inventories have a distinct scope: the questionnaire asks for inventories **warehoused in the United States, regardless of where manufactured**, to which the respondent holds title. It specifies the 50 states and District of Columbia. This distinction matters when studying imports, exports, reshoring, or supply chains. [5]

### What “broad-based” does—and does not—mean

“Broad-based” accurately describes coverage across manufacturing industries. It does **not** mean:

- every manufacturer reports each month;
- every six-digit NAICS industry is separately published;
- the panel proportionally represents small and large firms;
- the estimates describe employment, wages, profits, physical output, or community-level effects.

M3 is principally a **national dollar-value indicator**, with an especially important role in monitoring changes over time.

---

## 2. Publisher, stewardship, and institutional responsibility

The **U.S. Census Bureau**, within the **Department of Commerce**, collects, processes, and publishes M3.

Recent publications identify the responsible office as:

> Economic Indicators Division, Shipments, Inventories, and Orders Branch (M3)

Published data-inquiry contacts include:

- **Email:** `eid.m3.qs@census.gov`
- **Telephone:** **301-763-4832**

Census is the authoritative producer. Other institutions—particularly the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis through FRED—redistribute selected series. Their series identifiers, update timestamps, transformations, and historical coverage should not be confused with Census’s original publication metadata. [4, 15]

The Bureau of Economic Analysis, Federal Reserve Board, Treasury, and Council of Economic Advisers are important **users**, not the primary publishers.

---

## 3. Legal authority, mandate, and confidentiality

### 3.1 Statutory authority

The July 2026 Federal Register notice cites:

- **13 U.S.C. § 131:** Establishes collection and publication of periodic economic censuses, including manufactures.
- **13 U.S.C. § 182:** Authorizes surveys furnishing annual and other interim current data on subjects covered by those censuses.
- **13 U.S.C. § 193:** Authorizes preliminary and supplementary statistics related to census subjects. [3, 6]

**Important distinction:** These statutes establish authority for economic-statistics collection. They should not be described as a standalone statute expressly requiring a monthly survey named “M3.”

### 3.2 Voluntary reporting

The monthly M3 survey’s respondent obligation is **voluntary**. This is explicitly stated in the current Federal Register notice and recent Census publications.

It is therefore incorrect to assume that all Census business surveys are mandatory, or that the Economic Census’s reporting requirements automatically apply to M3. [3, 4]

### 3.3 Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

M3 operates under the **Paperwork Reduction Act** and OMB clearance:

- **OMB control number:** 0607-0008
- **Form:** M-3(SD)

The July 20, 2026 notice proposes extending the currently approved collection without change. It estimates:

| Burden measure | Estimate |
|---|---:|
| Respondents | 5,000 |
| Annual reports | 60,000 |
| Time per response | 20 minutes |
| Annual reporting burden | 20,000 hours |
| Additional annual costs to respondents | $0, excluding the cost of respondents’ time |

These are **clearance/burden estimates**, not a count of actual responding companies in a particular month. [3]

### 3.4 Principal federal economic indicator requirements

OMB has designated M3 a **principal federal economic indicator**. Its release arrangements are governed by **Statistical Policy Directive No. 3**, concerning compilation, release, and evaluation of principal federal economic indicators.

This matters because M3 is market-sensitive information whose release timing affects policymakers, businesses, investors, and the public. The 2026 notice explains how OMB approved earlier publication of total-manufacturing estimates. [3, 16]

### 3.5 Confidentiality and disclosure protection

**13 U.S.C. § 9** requires Census to keep respondent information confidential and use it for statistical purposes. Census cannot publicly release responses in a way that identifies a business, organization, or institution.

The methodology describes:

- **Primary suppressions:** Cells withheld because they could reveal confidential information.
- **Complementary suppressions:** Additional cells withheld to prevent users from reconstructing primary suppressed values.
- Disclosure review before release.

The current documentation cites disclosure-review approval **CBDRB-FY26-0151**.

Census also states that submitted data are protected through cybersecurity screening under the **Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015**. [2, 4, 7]

**Preservation implication:** Public aggregate statistics can be archived openly. Confidential respondent records cannot be treated as an open-data preservation target.

## 4. What M3 measures

| Measure | Meaning | Analytical interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Shipments** | Dollar value of products sold/shipped by domestic manufacturing operations | Current sales/deliveries and industrial activity |
| **New orders** | New commitments received during the month, net of cancellations and contract modifications | Indicator of future production commitments |
| **Unfilled orders** | End-of-month backlog of orders not yet recorded through the sales account | Outstanding production commitments |
| **Total inventories** | End-of-month inventory value | Stocks held relative to demand and shipments |
| **Materials and supplies** | Unprocessed raw and semifabricated inputs and supplies owned by the respondent | Input stocks |
| **Work in process** | Accumulated costs of goods undergoing fabrication and applicable undelivered contract work | Production in progress |
| **Finished goods** | Completed products ready for shipment and applicable resale goods | Completed output awaiting sale/delivery |

Shipments generally use net selling values **free on board plant**, after discounts and allowances, excluding freight charges and excise taxes. Some industries conventionally report delivered prices instead. Transfers between reporting units are included at their economic value. [5, 7]

Inventory reporting excludes nonmanufacturing activities and requires values before the **LIFO reserve adjustment** where applicable. The questionnaire also instructs respondents not to deduct progress billings from inventory values. These accounting conventions matter when comparing M3 with corporate financial statements. [5]

### Orders are not collected uniformly across industries

Census does not request orders from industries characterized mainly by immediate deliveries. Consequently, “orders” should not be interpreted as an equally detailed, independently observed measure for every manufacturing industry.

For universe estimates, Census derives new orders using:

\[
N_t = S_t + (U_t-U_{t-1})
\]

where \(N\) is new orders, \(S\) is shipments, and \(U\) is unfilled orders.

This includes orders received and filled in the same month and the effects of cancellations and modifications. **Published new orders are therefore not simply the sum of all reported new-order responses.** [2, 8]

### Additional published series

Products also include:

- durable and nondurable manufacturing aggregates;
- totals excluding transportation or defense;
- capital-goods and other topical groupings;
- inventories-to-shipments ratios;
- unfilled-orders-to-shipments ratios;
- percentage changes and revision tables.

These aggregates often overlap. They must not all be added together.

## 5. Survey design and production methods

### 5.1 Population, panel, and reporting units

The methodology identifies the manufacturing universe using the most recent Economic Census.

For the **2022 Economic Census**, it reports approximately:

- **250,000 manufacturing companies**;
- **299,000 establishments**;
- **1,700 companies** exceeding $500 million in manufacturing shipments.

The target sample includes companies with at least **$500 million in annual manufacturing shipments**, plus a supplemental panel of smaller manufacturers.

Recent publications describe approximately:

- **3,000 companies**;
- **4,700 reporting units**;
- **92 industry categories**, combined into **65 publication levels** because of the small monthly panel. [2, 4]

A company with diversified operations may report separately for divisions in different industries. A reporting unit can encompass multiple plants and activities outside its assigned M3 category.

**This is fundamentally different from an establishment-by-establishment census.**

### 5.2 Coverage indicators

The June 2026 full report states that companies with shipments **reported or imputed** represent approximately **58%** of manufacturing shipment value in the 2022 Economic Census.

Companies with shipments **actually reported** represent approximately **38%**.

These figures:

- are value-of-shipments coverage measures;
- are not conventional respondent-count response rates;
- distinguish actual reported information from reported-plus-imputed coverage. [4]

### 5.3 Collection methods

The 2026 Federal Register notice states:

- collection is primarily through the internet;
- respondents are initially contacted by email, with a small subset receiving mailed letters;
- data can be submitted through the internet or email;
- reminder emails and telephone calls support reporting;
- **paper collection was phased out beginning in January 2026**. [3]

Older overview pages describe fax capture and “Census Taker.” Those should be retained as historical documentation, not accepted as the current collection workflow.

### 5.4 Estimation and imputation

Census uses a **link-relative procedure** for shipments, total inventories, and unfilled orders:

1. Determine the ratio of current-month to prior-month values among units present in both months.
2. Apply that ratio to the previous universe estimate.
3. Handle unusually large or atypical company movements separately so they do not improperly drive estimates for nonrespondents and firms outside the panel.

Missing information is imputed using **company or industry historical trends**.

The central assumption is that month-to-month movements of reporting units appropriately represent movements of the larger industry universe. [2]

### 5.5 Inventory stage-of-fabrication estimates

Some companies report total inventories but cannot provide all fabrication stages.

Census therefore estimates stages at the three-digit NAICS subsector level and controls their sum to estimated total inventories, allocating differences proportionally. Stage-of-fabrication estimates should not be assumed to be entirely direct observations. [2]

### 5.6 Seasonal adjustment

Census uses **X-13ARIMA-SEATS** to remove predictable seasonal and calendar-related patterns.

Detailed shipments, unfilled orders, and total inventories are seasonally adjusted. Seasonally adjusted new orders are derived from adjusted shipments and the change in adjusted unfilled orders.

Published notes describe trading-day and holiday adjustments where appropriate, and adjustments for non-calendar reporting. **“Not seasonally adjusted” does not necessarily mean untouched raw questionnaire data.** [2, 4]

## 6. Reliability, uncertainty, and appropriate interpretation

### The critical statistical limitation

The current panel is **not a probability sample**.

Census explicitly states that:

- sampling error cannot be measured;
- conventional confidence intervals cannot be computed;
- statistical significance of published changes is not measurable for this survey. [2, 4]

A published monthly change should not be presented as “statistically significant” on the basis of an official M3 sampling margin of error—there is no such margin.

Researchers may estimate uncertainty in their own models, but that is different from Census quantifying the survey’s sampling error.

### Other important limitations

1. **Large-firm dependence.** Large-company movements may differ from those of small manufacturers.
2. **Nonresponse and imputation.** Published totals partly depend on modeled missing information.
3. **Reporting-unit mismatch.** Company/division data are used to estimate an establishment-based manufacturing universe.
4. **Coverage, response, and processing errors.** Editing reduces important errors but does not eliminate them.
5. **Nominal values.** Growth may reflect prices rather than greater physical production.
6. **Volatility.** Aircraft and other large transportation orders can dominate monthly movements.
7. **Cancellations and contract changes.** Orders are commitments, not guaranteed future production.
8. **Revisions.** Initial estimates are not final.
9. **Limited local and distributional detail.** M3 alone cannot establish effects on a state, town, demographic group, or small-business population.

**Good practice:** Evaluate several months, industry detail, and complementary sources rather than treating one headline monthly change as definitive evidence.

| **Subsequent years** | Selection emphasis shifted from employment to shipment value, with additional recruitment of large companies and undercovered industries. |
| **1990** | A roughly 400-company midsize-plastics probability sample tested feasibility in an industry with smaller firms. |
| **2001** | Revised January 1992–March 2001 monthly estimates released on a NAICS basis, replacing SIC-based classification for contemporary products. |
| **2007** | Approximately 380 nonreporting companies added through an augmentation project. |
| **April 2010 reports onward** | Separate semiconductor-industry estimates discontinued, while applicable values remain in broader aggregates. |
| **October 2021** | Advance total-manufacturing and nondurable aggregate estimates accelerated to the durable-goods advance-release timing. |
| **2024** | OMB clearance incorporated early-release provisions; additional nondurable industry detail added. |
| **July 2025** | Advance Total Manufacturing expanded to detailed shipments and inventories for all nondurable industries, beginning with June 2025 data. |
| **January 2026** | Paper collection phased out. |
| **2026** | Census announced that historical revisions and seasonal-model updates would remain unchanged for the remainder of the year because of schedule/resource constraints. |

Sources: Census methodology, historical revision documentation, historical-series page, and the 2026 Federal Register notice. [2, 3, 9, 10]

### Different meanings of “start date”

Do not assign one starting date to every M3 resource:

- **1957:** Census’s stated monthly survey-operation start.
- **1958–2001:** Historical SIC time-series coverage identified on the Census website.
- **1992 onward:** Main modern NAICS-era historical coverage, subject to series-specific availability.
- **Earlier related statistics:** Older manufacturing inventory series appear in historical publications and the NBER Macrohistory Database. These are not automatically equivalent to contemporary M3 definitions.

For example, FRED’s total-manufacturing new-orders series **AMTMNO** starts in **February 1992**, demonstrating why coverage must be recorded per series rather than inferred from the program’s age. [9, 15]

## 8. Release schedule, revisions, and benchmarking

### Regular products

| Product | Normal timing | Content |
|---|---|---|
| **Advance durable-goods report** | Approximately 18 working days after month-end; **8:30 a.m. Eastern** | Early durable-goods estimates |
| **Advance Total Manufacturing estimates** | Same advance-release stage | Earlier total and nondurable estimates; detailed nondurable shipments/inventories now included |
| **Full manufacturing report** | Approximately 23 working days after month-end; **10:00 a.m. Eastern** | More detailed durable and nondurable data, including late receipts |
| **Benchmark revision products** | Periodic comprehensive releases, historically annual | Revised levels, histories, and seasonal adjustments |

Use the actual release calendar, not the approximate lag, when building a historical information timeline. [3, 11]

### Revisions

Recent report notes describe:

- corrections incorporated in the full report;
- subsequent corrections appearing in the next advance report;
- revisions beyond the short monthly revision window reflected in benchmark publications.

Preserve the **advance**, **full**, and later revised values separately. “Full report” does not mean “permanently final.” [4]

### Benchmark dependencies

M3’s monthly movements are periodically aligned with broader annual information:

- Economic Census;
- Annual Survey of Manufactures;
- Manufacturers’ Unfilled Orders Survey, or M3UFO.

The **May 16, 2025 benchmark release** revised:

- seasonally adjusted data from **January 2012 through March 2025**;
- not seasonally adjusted data from **January 2017 through March 2025**.

It benchmarked shipments and inventories to the **2022 Economic Census** and revised 2018–2021 ASM data, incorporated unfilled-orders ratios, corrected reported data, and updated seasonal adjustments. It explicitly used a **2017 NAICS basis**. [12]

### Transition to AIES

The **Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES)** replaced several annual surveys, including ASM and M3UFO, beginning with reference year 2023; data collection began in March 2024.

**The monthly M3 survey itself was not replaced by AIES.** The transition affects its annual benchmarking environment and should be documented in long-term preservation and comparability records. [8, 14]

## 9. Typical users and public benefits

### Documented users

| User | Typical use |
|---|---|
| **Bureau of Economic Analysis** | GDP estimates, including manufacturing-related shipments and inventories inputs |
| **Federal Reserve Board** | Monitoring economic activity and informing monetary policy |
| **Treasury and Council of Economic Advisers** | Economic assessment and fiscal-policy development |
| **The Conference Board** | Orders inputs to the Leading Economic Index |
| **Manufacturers and corporate economists** | Demand forecasts, production planning, inventory management |
| **Trade associations** | Industry monitoring and comparison |
| **Investment analysts and consultants** | Business-cycle and capital-spending assessment |
| **Academics and researchers** | Forecasting, manufacturing cycles, inventories, supply-chain behavior |
| **News media** | Reporting on factory orders and the economy |

These uses are described by Census and Federal Register documentation. [7, 16]

### Public benefits

M3’s public value extends beyond financial markets:

- **A shared evidence base:** Publicly released statistics allow different parties to assess manufacturing conditions using the same underlying indicators.
- **Earlier warning of changing conditions:** Orders, backlogs, and inventory relationships can signal future expansion or weakness.
- **Better policy information:** Policymakers need timely statistics rather than relying solely on delayed annual data.
- **Business planning:** Firms can compare their own experiences with broader industry movements.
- **Public accountability:** Journalists, advocates, and citizens can evaluate claims about manufacturing performance.
- **Historical understanding:** Long series help document recessions, recoveries, disruptions, and structural change.

These are benefits of the information infrastructure; they are **not evidence that any particular policy or business decision made using M3 was successful**.

### Policy-activist uses and cautions

M3 can contribute to research on industrial policy, tariffs, defense demand, supply bottlenecks, or reshoring. However:

- orders do not equal jobs;
- nominal shipments do not equal real output;
- domestic manufacturing does not mean domestic ownership;
- national industry growth does not establish local benefits;
- M3 alone cannot attribute a change to a policy.

Distributional or causal work requires additional data and an appropriate research design.

## 11. Confidential microdata access

Business-level M3 data are available through a **restricted-use research pathway**, not public downloads.

Census’s restricted-use economic-data inventory lists:

- **Dataset:** M3
- **Frequency:** Monthly
- **Unit:** Firm
- **Listed availability:** **1992–2024**
- **Sponsor:** Census Bureau

External access requires an approved research project and authorization for the specific data through the **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)**.

Applications use the **Standard Application Process (SAP)**. Census says SAP is the definitive current availability catalog; the general inventory is not a guarantee that every listed year is immediately usable.

Many economic datasets contain Federal Tax Information, potentially requiring IRS approval. Exact requirements depend on the requested data and project. [14]

**Preservation distinction:** An independent archive can preserve public M3 releases. Confidential source-data preservation and access remain governed by Census’s secure infrastructure and legal controls.

## 12. Guidance for data scientists

### Recommended data model

Use a long-format table with at least:

```text
reference_month
geography
industry_or_category_code
classification_system
classification_vintage
measure
seasonal_adjustment_status
value
unit
publication_stage
release_datetime
retrieval_datetime
source_url
revision_status
suppression_or_missing_status
benchmark_vintage
```

For forecasting and policy evaluation, **reference month** and **release date** must remain separate.

### Essential controls

1. **Avoid look-ahead bias.** Use historically available vintages for real-time forecasting tests.
2. **Do not sum overlapping aggregates.**
3. **Separate stocks from flows.** Shipments/orders can be summed over periods; end-of-month inventories/backlogs should not be summed as though they were monthly output.
4. **Do not assume seasonal adjustment implies annualization.**
5. **Do not replace suppressed or unavailable values with zero.**
6. **Record classification basis.** The Economic Census reference year does not necessarily identify the NAICS vintage used in a release.
7. **Use matching vintages for identities and ratios.** Mixing revised shipments with unrevised backlogs can create artificial discrepancies.
8. **Check nominal versus real interpretation.** Document any external deflator.
9. **Retain source footnotes.** They contain substantive coverage and comparability information.
10. **Check both headline and less volatile components.** Especially for transportation and capital goods.

### Complementary datasets

Depending on the question, useful companions include:

- Federal Reserve industrial production and capacity utilization;
- BLS producer prices and manufacturing employment;
- Economic Census and AIES;
- international trade statistics;
- BEA national and regional accounts;
- Census retail and wholesale inventories;
- business-demography datasets for small-firm and ownership questions.

These measure different concepts and should be joined with explicit definitions.

## 13. Preservation and library recommendations

### Preserve a collection, not a single download

A sound M3 preservation package should include:

1. Every advance and full report in original form.
2. Associated spreadsheets and tables.
3. Snapshots of historical-series downloads and API responses.
4. Benchmark releases and revision explanations.
5. Questionnaires and reporting instructions.
6. Methodology and definitions.
7. Industry composition tables and SIC–NAICS conversion documentation.
8. Release calendars, corrections, and special notices.
9. API variable metadata, examples, and code dictionaries.
10. PRA notices and relevant clearance documentation.

### Main preservation risks

| Risk | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Mutable “current” URLs** | The same URL can serve different releases over time |
| **Revised historical downloads** | Earlier values disappear from the latest series |
| **Stale documentation** | Overview pages can contradict contemporary releases |
| **Classification changes** | Identically named industries may not remain comparable |
| **API authentication/interface changes** | Automated capture can fail |
| **Format and accessibility issues** | PDFs may be difficult to extract reliably; spreadsheets need schema interpretation |
| **Resource constraints** | Benchmarking and seasonal-model maintenance can be deferred |
| **Annual benchmark-source transitions** | AIES changes the surrounding statistical production system |

### Practical archival workflow

- Capture each publication stage when released.
- Store immutable raw files alongside normalized derivatives.
- Record URLs, retrieval time, release time, file size, format, and **SHA-256 checksum**.
- Preserve web pages as well as linked files.
- Validate expected files against the release calendar.
- Run regression checks on units, schemas, totals, and series identities.
- Maintain versioned code and an ingestion log.
- Keep separate collections for “latest revised history” and “as originally released.”
- Assign repository persistent identifiers and publish clear provenance.

**Suggested citation:**

> U.S. Census Bureau. *Manufacturers’ Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3)*, [product/table/series], [reference period], released [date], [advance/full/benchmark vintage], [adjustment status and units]. Retrieved [date] from [URL].

### Unresolved archival questions

The sources reviewed did **not** establish:

- an M3-specific NARA records-retention schedule or accession history;
- a complete inventory of surviving pre-web publications;
- a guarantee that every original spreadsheet or API vintage remains preserved;
- a program-specific annual operating budget;
- a comprehensive current audit of publication accessibility.

These require follow-up with Census, NARA, federal depository libraries, or repository stewards. A long historical series on a website is not itself proof of comprehensive archival preservation.

## 15. Corrections and qualifications to common descriptions

Your supplied description requires no correction. However, a complete catalog record should avoid these common errors:

| Claim | Correct qualification |
|---|---|
| “M3 is mandatory.” | Monthly M3 participation is voluntary. |
| “Only firms above $500 million are included.” | Large firms are the target emphasis; a supplemental smaller-firm panel also exists. |
| “M3 publishes every six-digit NAICS industry.” | Collection categories are combined into fewer publication levels. |
| “M3 currently covers 89 categories.” | Recent publications describe 92 categories and 65 publication levels; the older overview is stale. |
| “Data are collected by fax and paper.” | The 2026 notice describes internet/email collection and paper phaseout. |
| “Only durable goods are available at the advance stage.” | Advance Total Manufacturing now includes detailed nondurable shipments and inventories. |
| “New orders are directly summed from questionnaires.” | Universe estimates are derived from shipments and backlog changes. |
| “The data are inflation-adjusted.” | They are not adjusted for price changes. |
| “58% is the response rate.” | It is reported-or-imputed shipment-value coverage against the Economic Census. |
| “The full report is final.” | Monthly and benchmark revisions can follow. |
| “AIES replaced M3.” | AIES replaced annual benchmark-source surveys, not monthly M3. |
| “2026 updates stopped.” | The notice concerns historical revisions and seasonal-model maintenance, not a cessation of monthly releases. |

## Bottom line

**M3 is high-value federal statistical infrastructure and a strong preservation priority.** Its combination of timely shipments, inventories, orders, and backlogs supports economic policy, GDP estimation, business planning, journalism, and historical research.

Its greatest strengths are **timeliness, continuity, industry breadth, and public availability**. Its principal weaknesses are **nonprobability sampling, large-firm dependence, nonresponse/imputation, nominal-dollar interpretation, limited local detail, and revisions**.

For preservationists and data librarians, the central task is to preserve **what was published, when, under which definitions and methods**—not merely today’s revised historical series.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.

- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.

# M3 dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Primary publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce  
**Primary location:** [Manufacturers’ Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3)](https://www.census.gov/manufacturing/m3/index.html)

## Overall assessment

**M3 remains publicly available and operational. I found no evidence of a decision to remove its historical archive or terminate the monthly survey. However, there are documented disruptions to publication and statistical maintenance, and substantial agency-wide staffing losses.**

The strongest dataset-specific warning is Census’s announcement that **historical revisions and seasonal-adjustment model updates will remain unchanged for the remainder of 2026 because of schedule and resource constraints**. The 2025 federal shutdown also demonstrably delayed M3 releases.

These findings indicate greater risk of **delayed or less thoroughly maintained statistics** than of outright disappearance. Public redistribution through FRED provides some protection against loss of existing series, but cannot replace future Census collection or preserve every original release.

### How the rubric is applied

- This assessment considers developments **since January 2025**, including disruptions that have subsequently been resolved.
- Agency-wide staffing evidence is identified separately from M3-specific evidence.
- Proposed budgets are distinguished from enacted appropriations.
- Ordinary statistical revisions are not treated as improper alteration or removal.
- “No Known Issue” means no qualifying problem was identified—not that every historical file was exhaustively audited.
- The rubric’s categories overlap. Where that matters, the reasoning below makes the interpretation explicit.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | **Not supported.** Census continues to provide historical reports and time series. |
| **High Risk** | **Not established.** I found no documented recent removal of pre-2026 M3 data files. This was not a complete file-by-file archive audit. |
| **Moderate Risk** | Census documents an older reduction: separate semiconductor-industry estimates were discontinued beginning with April 2010 reports. That is a longstanding publication limitation, not evidence that previously published historical records have recently been deleted. |
| **No Known Issue** | The [full-report archive](https://www.census.gov/manufacturing/m3/historical_data/) lists reports back to 1992. The [historical time-series page](https://www.census.gov/manufacturing/m3/historical/timeseries.html) retains NAICS series, revision documentation, and SIC series for 1958–2001. Recent 2025 reports remain discoverable in the archive. |

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

Historical access remains available, with no verified recent removal.

**Qualification:** The latest historical time series incorporate legitimate revisions and are not substitutes for original release vintages. Preservation should include archived reports as well as revised series. The 2026 suspension of historical revision work is a quality concern, not evidence of historical removal.

**Confidence:** Moderate; archive existence is well documented, but completeness has not been exhaustively tested.

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | **Not supported.** Monthly releases continue, and Census is seeking continued clearance. |
| **High Risk** | No M3-specific statutory publication deadline violation, permanently omitted monthly publication, or clearance expired for more than one year was identified. Collection was interrupted during the shutdown, but subsequent October 2025 estimates were published; this supports delay rather than a permanently skipped reference period. |
| **Moderate Risk** | **Directly supported by missed intended publication dates.** Census’s [release-update notice](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USCENSUS/bulletins/3fb7110) moved the August 2025 full report from **October 2 to November 18, 2025** because of the funding lapse. September’s advance report appeared November 26, and October’s advance report December 23—well beyond the usual approximately 18-working-day lag. |
| **No Known Issue** | Current evidence is reassuring: [OMB’s clearance record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202312-0607-002) lists M3 as **Active**, expiring **March 31, 2027**. The [July 2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-20/html/2026-14513.htm) proposes an extension **without change**. The August 2026 full report was released October 2, matching the [current calendar](https://www.census.gov/manufacturing/m3/release_schedule.html). |

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The rubric explicitly assigns Moderate Risk when typical or intended publication dates are missed. That happened, even though publication has recovered and clearance remains active.

This is **not evidence of imminent termination**. If the category were restricted solely to the latest release cycle, the on-schedule August 2026 release would support No Known Issue.

**Confidence:** High.
